_readme: Ground-truth corpus for non-latin-tagger. Each case gives raw HTML/text input plus the expected tagged runs. 'expectedRuns' lists every substring the tool should wrap in <span lang="xx">, in order. 'langCandidates' lists ISO 639-1/639-3 codes the disambiguation layer should consider, with the first entry being the expected default. 'ambiguityNote' flags cases where script alone can't determine language — these are the hardest, most important cases to test against. 'numbersToggleRelevant' flags cases where output differs depending on the includeNumbers setting.

cases.description: English sentence with embedded Urdu phrase, includes distinguishing Urdu letters (ں ھ ے) and trailing comma that must stay inside the run
cases.input: She greeted me with آپ کیسے ہیں، شکریہ, then switched back to English.

expectedRuns.ambiguityNote: Contains ھ and ے — distinguishing Urdu letters not present in standard Arabic. Heuristic should resolve to ur with high confidence.

cases.description: English sentence with embedded Arabic phrase, no Urdu/Persian-distinguishing letters present — genuinely ambiguous by character set alone
cases.input: The sign read مرحبا بكم في القاهرة and pointed toward the exit.

expectedRuns.ambiguityNote: No distinguishing letters present. This is the hard case: character-set heuristics alone cannot resolve it. Should fall through to statistical language ID or default to ar with a low-confidence flag for user review.

cases.description: English sentence with embedded Persian phrase, includes distinguishing letters (گ چ پ ژ)
cases.input: He whispered چگونه‌ای، دوست عزیز before leaving the room.

expectedRuns.ambiguityNote: Contains چ, گ — Persian-distinguishing letters. Heuristic should resolve to fa.

cases.description: English sentence with embedded Hindi (Devanagari) phrase including internal punctuation
cases.input: The teacher said, नमस्ते, कैसे हो? and waited for a reply.

expectedRuns.ambiguityNote: Devanagari is shared by Hindi, Marathi, Nepali, and Sanskrit. Default to hi as most common in publishing contexts unless corpus-level metadata (e.g., document language declaration) suggests otherwise.

cases.description: English sentence with embedded Hebrew phrase — near-unambiguous script-to-language mapping
cases.input: The inscription read שלום עליכם, welcoming all visitors.

expectedRuns.ambiguityNote: Hebrew script is also used for Yiddish, but modern Hebrew vocabulary/orthography here makes he the safe default. Yiddish would show distinct spelling conventions (e.g., different vowel-pointing patterns).

cases.description: English sentence with embedded Simplified Chinese phrase
cases.input: The menu listed 北京烤鸭 as the house specialty.

expectedRuns.ambiguityNote: Han script is shared with Japanese kanji. Absence of hiragana/katakana and presence of simplified character forms should resolve this to zh-Hans.

cases.description: English sentence with Japanese phrase mixing kanji, hiragana, and katakana — tests that mixed-script runs within one language stay unified
cases.input: She wrote ありがとうございます、スミスさん in her notebook.

expectedRuns.text: ありがとうございます、スミスさん
expectedRuns.ambiguityNote: Presence of hiragana/katakana alongside any kanji is a strong, near-unambiguous signal for Japanese even though Han-only substrings would be ambiguous with Chinese.

cases.description: English sentence with embedded Korean (Hangul) phrase — unambiguous script-to-language mapping
cases.input: The sign above the door read 환영합니다 in bold letters.

expectedRuns.ambiguityNote: Hangul is used exclusively for Korean; no disambiguation needed.

cases.description: English sentence with embedded Thai phrase including internal punctuation-like tone marks
cases.input: The vendor smiled and said สวัสดีค่ะ, ยินดีต้อนรับ warmly.

expectedRuns.text: สวัสดีค่ะ, ยินดีต้อนรับ
expectedRuns.ambiguityNote: Thai script is unambiguous. Tests that combining tone marks stay attached to base consonants via grapheme clustering.

cases.description: English sentence with embedded Russian phrase — Cyrillic ambiguity case (Russian vs. Ukrainian vs. Bulgarian vs. Serbian)
cases.input: The note simply said Привет, как дела? and nothing more.

expectedRuns.ambiguityNote: No і, ї, є, ґ (Ukrainian-distinguishing letters) present, and no ъ-heavy Bulgarian patterns. Should resolve to ru by default/statistical fallback; this is a good stress test for the same disambiguation architecture used for Arabic-script languages.

cases.description: Cyrillic phrase containing Ukrainian-distinguishing letters (і, ї, є) to test the Cyrillic disambiguation heuristic
cases.input: На вулиці було тихо і темно, як завжди ввечері.

expectedRuns.text: На вулиці було тихо і темно, як завжди ввечері.
expectedRuns.ambiguityNote: Contains і and ї — letters not used in standard Russian orthography. Heuristic should resolve to uk with high confidence.

cases.description: Arabic phrase followed directly by Western Arabic numerals — primary test case for the numbers-include/exclude toggle
cases.input: الفصل رقم 12 يبدأ من هنا.
cases.ambiguityNote: With includeNumbers=true, '12' should NOT split the run since Western digits sit inline within Arabic text. With includeNumbers=false, the digit sequence should break the run into two separate spans.

cases.description: Arabic phrase using native Eastern Arabic-Indic numerals instead of Western digits
cases.input: الصفحة ١٢ من الكتاب.
cases.ambiguityNote: Eastern Arabic-Indic digits (٠-٩) report their own script (Arabic), so they merge into the run regardless of the numbers toggle; functionally 'numbers within the run.' Confirms the numbers toggle treats both digit systems consistently. Also tests that the numeral system itself isn't a disambiguation signal on its own (both Arabic and Urdu texts commonly use either digit system).

cases.description: English sentence with a quoted non-Latin phrase — tests that quotation marks immediately adjacent to the run don't get incorrectly absorbed or incorrectly excluded
cases.input: He asked what "तुम कैसे हो" meant in English.

expectedRuns.ambiguityNote: Punctuation touching a non-Latin run always attaches to it, regardless of what is on the far side, so the surrounding straight quotes are part of the run. Whitespace is different: it only joins when both sides match.

cases.description: Single sentence with two different non-Latin scripts in sequence, testing that runs break cleanly at the script boundary rather than merging
cases.input: The label showed both مرحبا and 你好 side by side on the poster.
cases.ambiguityNote: Tests that the run-builder correctly terminates a run when script changes, even with only a single Latin word ('and') separating them.

cases.description: Arabic-script phrase in Sindhi, which has its own extended letter set (ڪ, ڏ, ڊ, ڀ, ٺ) beyond both Arabic and Urdu
cases.input: هي ڪتاب تمام سٺو آهي.

expectedRuns.ambiguityNote: Contains ڪ and ٺ — Sindhi-specific letters absent from both Arabic and Urdu. Tests that the disambiguation table extends beyond the three most common Arabic-script languages and doesn't force a mis-tag to ur just because Sindhi letters superficially resemble Urdu's extended set.

cases.description: Arabic-script phrase in Pashto, with distinguishing letters (ږ, ښ, ځ, ډ)
cases.input: ته څنګه یې، زما ملګریه؟

expectedRuns.ambiguityNote: Contains څ and ږ — Pashto-specific letters. Good regression test alongside case 16 to confirm the heuristic table doesn't collapse all 'extra Arabic-script letters' into a single generic bucket.

cases.description: Very short Arabic-script run (a single common word) with no distinguishing letters and too little text for statistical language ID to work reliably
cases.input: He simply said شكرا and walked away.

expectedRuns.ambiguityNote: Deliberately adversarial: too short for n-gram statistical models to have real signal, and 'thank you' is a common loanword across Arabic, Urdu, and Persian speech. This case should trigger a low-confidence flag and surface the language picker to the user rather than silently guessing.

cases.description: Devanagari phrase using classical/liturgical vocabulary and conjuncts typical of Sanskrit rather than conversational Hindi
cases.input: अथ योगानुशासनम् इति पतञ्जलिना उक्तम्।

expectedRuns.ambiguityNote: Heavy conjunct consonant clusters and the danda (।) punctuation mark are strong statistical signals for Sanskrit over conversational Hindi. Tests whether the statistical fallback (not just character-set heuristics, since the alphabet is identical) correctly shifts the default away from hi.

cases.description: A non-Latin run that contains an embedded Latin-script proper noun (e.g., a brand name), testing run-breaking behavior at a hard boundary case
cases.input: أعلنت شركة Google عن تحديث جديد اليوم.
cases.ambiguityNote: The Latin brand name 'Google' should break the Arabic run into two spans rather than being absorbed into either — proper nouns/brand names are Latin script and should never be force-included in a non-Latin span. This is the trickiest run-boundary case in the corpus and worth extra unit tests.
